b) It stands to reason that not only the interests of the claimant but also the severity of the fault 
should be assessed in light of the damage incurred. However, this does not mean that a 
contractual penalty is excessive merely because it exceeds the amount that the entitled party 
could claim as damages for the breach of contract. Consequently, it is not the actual damage 
incurred but the maximum possible damage that serves as an indicator of excessiveness (BGE 
103 II 109; MERZ, ZBJV 115/1979, p. 283). The contractual penalty is the subject of an 
independent obligation that must be distinguished from liability for damages; this is already 
evident from the fact that, pursuant to Art. 161(1) OR, it becomes due even if the creditor has not 
suffered any damage. 
Finally, it should be noted that it is not the creditor who must demonstrate the reasonableness of 
the contractual penalty, but rather the debtor who must assert and prove the conditions for a 
reduction (BGE 103 II 109 with references). 
For a much more recent case by the Swiss Federal Court, see the decision dated September 24, 
2024 (translated with Deepl) 
4.1.2. The parties may set the contractual penalty at any amount they choose. The judge must 
reduce excessively high contractual penalties at his or her discretion. 
When reducing a contractual penalty at the court’s discretion, restraint is required for reasons of 
good faith and freedom of contract (Art. 163(1) OR). Judicial intervention in the contract is 
justified only if the agreed-upon amount is so high that it exceeds the reasonable limit still 
compatible with justice and equity (BGE 133 III 201 E. 5.2, 43 E. 3.3.1). A reduction of the 
contractual penalty is justified in particular where there is a gross disproportion between the 
agreed amount and the claimant’s interest, at the time of the breach, in enforcing it in full. 
Whether this condition is met is not determined on a general basis but depends on the 
circumstances of the individual case. These include, in particular, the nature and duration of the 
contract, the severity of the fault and the breach of contract, the other party’s interest in enforcing 
the prohibition, and the financial situation of the parties involved, particularly the obligated 
party. Furthermore, any dependencies arising from the contractual relationship and the business 
experience of the parties must be taken into account. A reduction is more readily justified in
